title: Population imaging of synaptically released glutamate in mouse hippocampal slices
protocol: Arrange all slices in a holding chamber.
Place the holding chamber under an upright widefield epifluorescence microscope with low magnification and large working distance.
Use white light for initial inspection of the slice holding chamber.
Illuminate slices with blue laser or halogen lamp equipped with GFP filter set.
Select slices which show fluorescence in the target region (CA1 or CA3).
Bubble aCSF in the slice holding chamber constantly with carbogen.
Gently collect one selected brain slice with a Pasteur’s pipette and transfer it to the experiment chamber.
Secure the position of the slice in the chamber using a flattened platinum wire frame with a nylon fiber grid.
Keep remaining slices at room temperature in aCSF bubbled continuously with carbogen.
Set the excitation light wavelength to 920–940 nm for two-photon imaging.
Introduce a beam splitter (705 nm) into the light path to reflect emitted light into the photomultiplier tube.
Use a long working-distance 40× water-immersion objective for standard imaging recordings.
Equip an upright microscope with a 488 nm laser or laser diode for excitation.
Introduce a 505 nm beam splitter into the light path to guide the excitation light onto the sample.
Place a 520 nm longpass filter in front of the camera for detection of emitted light.
Mount an sCMOS ANDOR Zyla 4.2 camera on an Olympus BW51WI scope.
Use either an inverted camera objective with a focal length of 50 mm or a 20× water immersion objective.
Recommend imaging frame rates of 30–100 Hz for optimal sampling of synaptically-evoked glutamate transients.
Mount a slice perfusion system on a small stage and a micromanipulator for positioning the micropipette used for synaptic stimulation.
Add a second manipulator for electrophysiological recordings if needed.
Mount the experiment chamber to the stage under the objective of the microscope.
Start perfusion with warmed (34°C), carbogen-saturated aCSF (0.5–2 ml/min).
Illuminate the slice using a white LED placed near the recording chamber.
Lower the water-immersion microscope objective into the aCSF.
Adjust the focal plane until the slice surface becomes visible through the ocular of your microscope.
Locate the CA1 region by using the outline of the hippocampal slice and densely packed neuronal somata in the stratum pyramidale as guiding structures.
Turn on the single- or two-photon microscope.
Inspect the SF-iGluSnFR expression level in the stratum radiatum under single- or two-photon excitation, respectively.
Identify the region of interest with dense and homogenous expression of SF-iGluSnFR.
Set the focal plane at least 50 μm below the slice surface for two-photon imaging.
Keep laser intensity low to prevent phototoxicity.
Use a laser power below 15 mW (two-photon) and 1 mW (single-photon), when measured under the microscope’s objective.
Place a stimulation pipette filled with 2M NaCl solution below the objective using a micromanipulator.
Lower the pipette until it touches the slice surface.
Advance the pipette 50–100 μm below the slice surface with the tip in the stratum radiatum at a distance of 75–100 μm from the stratum pyramidale.
Mount another pipette filled with 2M NaCl to the headstage of your extracellular amplifier connected to a second micromanipulator.
Advance the pipette tip to a location 50–100 μm below the slice surface and 75–100 μm from the pyramidal layer.
Place the fEPSP electrode typically 100–150 μm away from the stimulation pipette towards CA3.
Place the reference electrode in the bath solution.
Center the field of view (FOV) to the area surrounding the tip of the fEPSP recording electrode.
Adjust the focal plane to a depth of about 100–150 μm below the surface.
Image a rectangular FOV with an edge length of about 60–120 μm.
Connect the stimulation pipette and the ground electrode to a stimulus isolator.
Deliver short pulses (80–100 μsec, 1 V) and monitor both the fluorescence changes in a region of interest covering the whole FOV.
Monitor the electrophysiological responses.
Repeat step 11 with increasing voltage levels.
Detect a population glutamate signal at stimulation strengths of 30-50 V.
Ensure single pulses evoke robust glutamate transients and fEPSPs without population spikes.
Avoid tissue damage by not exceeding a stimulation voltage of 60 V and do not increase the pulse duration.
Record 10-20 image series of 3–4 sec with the stimulation pulse delivered after one second of baseline registration.
Ensure stimuli are delivered at least 10 s apart to minimize activity-dependent plastic changes of synaptic responses.
Synchronize electrophysiological recordings with imaging if recording fEPSPs simultaneously.
If possible, record voltage traces in the imaging software for synchronization.
Create a voltage pulse in the imaging software and align it with the trigger signal from the electrophysiology setup.
For local drug application, use a glass pipette connected to a pressure application device containing the desired drug (e.g., TTX, 5 μM).
Place the pipette tip near the site of imaging, approximately 50–100 μm below the slice surface.
Record a series of sweeps under baseline conditions to ensure population glutamate signals remain stable.
Eject a small volume of the drug under visual control.
Readjust the focal plane to keep all previously imaged structures in the FOV.
Record a series of sweeps during the drug application.
Stop pressure application after recording.
Wait several minutes for the complete washout of the applied substances.
Record a third set of 10–20 sweeps after washout.
Retract all pipettes after imaging experiment completion.
Remove the experiment chamber from the microscope table.
